catalog_quote: 2.4 Stress 2.4.1 Stress in words with heavy sequences If a word contains only one heavy sequence (vCC or C), stress is usually on the vowel of the heavy sequence. Examples of stress in words with one heavy sequence vCC: m nṭaqih ‘area’; y šrab ‘he drinks’; naʔ st ‘I / you (msg) slept’; ... katīr ‘much, many’; ʔah li ‘families’. If a word contains more than one heavy sequence, stress is usually on the vowel of the last heavy sequence. Examples of words with two or more heavy sequences: xall ṣt ‘I finished’; ... qadd m ‘opposite’; qōnūn ‘law’; yizzawwaǧūn ‘they marry’. However, these cannot be considered strict rules, since many examples were recorded that go against them. There seem to be two main tendencies causing this variation, namely regression of stress and progression of stress. Especially the former seems to be quite widespread and persistent, causing forms such as ys wwun (← ysuwwūn) ‘they make’; ... the regression and progression of stress analysis is followed here for forms with heavy sequences. ... 2.4.2 Stress in words without heavy sequences In nouns and verbs of the pattern CvCvC, there is also variation in stress placement. Thus, one hears b lad ~ bal d ‘village’; w lad ~ wal d ‘boy’; ... In trisyllabic words of the pattern CvCvCv stress is always on the second syllable: baq rih ‘cow’; šaǧ rih ‘tree’; ... The only recorded exception is s waʔan ‘regardless whether’, which is invariably pronounced with stress on the first syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: When etymological *a appears in light syllables in RJA, it is frequently lengthened, e.g. xaṣāb ~ xṣāb 'Khasab', ṭarāf 'edge', samāk 'fish', ḥarəf > ḥārəf 'a toponym', ʾāməs 'yesterday', sānih 'year' [...] Confoundingly, RJA also has both regression and progression of stress for expressive purposes, e.g. sēlam > sēlām 'male given name' [...] Davey (2016, 63) and Bernabela (2011, 66) both account for such lengthened vowels as an effect of stress. Indeed, in the preponderance of cases in both languages, lengthening of *a occurs in stressed position. [...] either that lengthening of *a can take place in light syllables without reference to stress, or that the stress rule varies in Dhofari as it does in RJA.
new_statements.citation: Shockley, Mark D. 2024. Ruʾūs al-Jibāl Arabic in Context: A Proposal for an Expanded Typology of Southeastern Arabian Dialects. Journal of Semitic Studies 69(1): 643-669. doi:10.1093/jss/fgad026

Al-Saqqaf, 1999, 81)'; 'Davey (20…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given. The source only says that stress in Ruʾūs al-Jibāl Arabic (RJA) lengthens a short *a in a light syllable (xaṣāb, ṭarāf, samāk 'fish', sānih 'year', baqārih 'cow', ʾaqābih — i.e. stress on the lengthened syllable, often the final or penultimate one), that the stress rule 'varies' within RJA, and that speakers shift stress leftward or rightward for expressive purposes (sēlam > sēlām). The author explicitly calls for an acoustic study of word stress. The primary phonology, Bernabela 2011 (p. 66), is credited with the stress-lengthening analysis but could not be opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Expressive regression/progression of stress (sēlam > sēlām; taʾlāb 'fox' vs tālab in Jayakar); lengthening does not usually occur in CaCCaC forms; forms like qārīb 'close to', rāṣīf 'pavement' show lengthening outside the expected stressed syllable; vowel lengthening 'is in flux and seems less common among urbanized speakers'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from the author's own fieldwork text corpus (Ras Al Khaimah and Musandam villages, e.g. al-Jādī, al-Qayr) compared with Dhofari Arabic; stress is discussed only as a conditioning factor for vowel lengthening, not described as a system.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog shih1239 'Ru'us al-Jibal' = Shihhi (Šiḥḥī) Arabic = Musandam Arabic [ssh], spoken on the Musandam peninsula (Oman) and Ras Al Khaimah (UAE). The sources describe particular villages: Bernabela 2011 the inland variety of əlǦēdih / al-Jādī; Bettega & Gasparini 2022 the coastal town of Lima; Anonby & Bettega 2025 songs from Ḥabalēn on the north-east coast; Shockley 2024 uses 'Ruʾūs al-Jibāl Arabic (RJA)' as a cover term (with Ras Al Khaimah, al-Jādī and al-Qayr data) and treats the Kumzari-speaking Kumzar as a separate language (Kumzari, kumz1235). Jayakar's article (vol. 21 of JBBRAS; archive.org issue dated 1902, usually cited as 1904) is on the 'Shahee' (Shihuh) dialect generally. No source names a distinct glottocode for these village varieties.

sources.note: pp. 655-656: etymological *a in light syllables is frequently lengthened (xaṣāb, ṭarāf, samāk); Bernabela (2011, 66) and Davey (2016, 63) treat this as an effect of stress and 'in the preponderance of cases.. lengthening of *a occurs in stressed position'; RJA also has 'regression and progression of stress for expressive purposes' (sēlam > sēlām); 'the stress rule varies in Dhofari as it does in RJA'; an acoustic study of word stress is called for. No placement rule stated.
'Unstressed short /i/ and /u/ reduce to schwa [ə]' (phonology section sourced to Bernabela 2011); no stress placement rule.
